summary: This informational document proposes an incremental carrier-grade NAT approach for IPv6 transition as IPv4 addresses run out. Host-based methods did not meet every need, so the operator adds NAT in stages. It combines tunneling with NAT.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 6264 proposes a staged way for an ISP to add IPv6 service while keeping much of its existing IPv4 network in place. A home gateway and a provider-side CGN handle IPv4 traffic and carry IPv6 traffic through a tunnel.

questions: how does incremental cgn combine ipv4 nat with ipv6 tunneling
why can the same cgn device support multiple transition phases
how does ipv6 travel through an ipv4 isp network
subtitle: A staged IPv6 transition approach that combines IPv4 address sharing with IPv6-over-IPv4 tunnels.

tldr.problem: An ISP may need to share scarce IPv4 addresses while leaving much of its existing IPv4 network unchanged during the initial transition to IPv6.
tldr.mechanism: A dual-stack home gateway sends IPv4 traffic toward a dual-stack Carrier-Grade NAT and tunnels IPv6 traffic over IPv4 to that device, which handles the two traffic types accordingly.
tldr.outcome: The approach can provide IPv4 and IPv6 access in stages and reuse the home gateway and CGN as the provider changes its network. The RFC combines existing technologies and defines no new protocol.

facts.label: Main components
facts.value: Dual-stack home gateway and dual-stack CGN

facts.label: Core transition method
facts.value: IPv6-over-IPv4 tunnel plus IPv4 address translation

today: RFC 6264 is an Informational RFC published in June 2011. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; the document proposes combining existing transition technologies rather than defining a new protocol.

sections.title: A Gradual Path from IPv4 to IPv6
sections.content:
The RFC describes increasing pressure to address IPv4 exhaustion while deploying IPv6. Host-based transition methods alone may not meet every need, and users may not be able to configure or maintain them. Carrier-Grade NAT (CGN) can share IPv4 addresses, but using CGN alone does not advance IPv6 deployment.

RFC 6264 proposes an incremental CGN approach that combines IPv4-to-IPv4 address translation with IPv6-over-IPv4 tunneling. It is a deployment proposal that combines existing technologies; it does not define a new protocol or forwarding mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: An ISP may need to share IPv4 addresses before it can change its entire network. This proposal combines that address sharing with a way to provide IPv6 service during the transition.

sections.title: The Home Gateway and Provider CGN
sections.content:
The approach uses a dual-stack home gateway and a dual-stack CGN in the ISP network. The home gateway handles IPv4 and IPv6. For IPv4, it forwards traffic toward the CGN and may perform local address translation. For IPv6, it encapsulates packets in IPv4 and sends them through a tunnel to the CGN.

The CGN translates ordinary IPv4 traffic toward the IPv4 Internet. For tunneled IPv6 traffic, it removes the IPv4 encapsulation and forwards the original IPv6 packet toward the IPv6 Internet. The RFC discusses 6rd as a suitable low-operational-cost tunnel approach, and also mentions other tunnel technologies.
sections.plainLanguage: The home gateway wraps IPv6 packets inside IPv4 packets and sends them to the provider's CGN. The CGN removes that wrapper and forwards the IPv6 packets onward, while it translates ordinary IPv4 traffic.

sections.title: How IPv4 and IPv6 Packets Travel
sections.content:
An IPv4 packet from a home gateway reaches the CGN as an ordinary IPv4 packet. The CGN translates its source address to a public IPv4 address and records the mapping needed for return traffic. Existing IPv4 hosts can continue using the ISP network as before.

An IPv6 packet from a customer host is encapsulated by the home gateway and sent over the IPv4 network to the CGN. The CGN decapsulates it and forwards it to the IPv6 Internet. Return traffic is tunneled to the appropriate home gateway using stored mapping information. IPv4/IPv6 translation for communication between the two protocol families is discussed as a separate function and is outside this proposal's scope.
sections.plainLanguage: IPv4 packets use address translation at the provider. IPv6 packets cross the existing IPv4 network inside a tunnel, then continue as IPv6 after the CGN removes the outer IPv4 packet.

sections.title: Reusing Equipment as the Network Changes
sections.content:
The RFC describes an ISP enabling transition functions in stages. A provider could begin with IPv4 address sharing, then enable IPv6-over-IPv4 tunneling, and later move toward native dual-stack or IPv6-only routing. The same CGN and home gateway can support different phases through configuration changes or software updates.

In a dual-stack provider network, a home gateway can stop tunneling when it detects native IPv6 Router Advertisement or DHCPv6 traffic. In the described IPv6-only evolution, the provider can reconfigure the CGN and gateway to use other transition functions such as Dual Stack Lite. Regions of one ISP may be at different stages.
sections.plainLanguage: The ISP can enable different functions as its network changes instead of replacing both devices at every stage. Different regions can use different configurations while the transition proceeds.

sections.title: Limitations and Security Considerations
sections.content:
For IPv4, the approach inherits CGN address-sharing issues, including scaling and difficulty supporting inbound traffic at well-known ports. The RFC states that application-layer problems from double NAT are outside its scope. For IPv6, it recommends a tunnel MTU of at least 1500 bytes to avoid excessive fragmentation and path-MTU interactions.

The RFC says the approach adds no new CGN features and therefore introduces no new CGN security considerations. The tunnels run within one ISP between the home gateway and CGN. The document advises applying packet inspection and ingress filtering to IPv6 packets after decapsulation and says the home gateway needs basic IPv6 security functions.
sections.plainLanguage: IPv4 address sharing retains CGN limitations, while IPv6 tunnel traffic needs appropriate checks after it is unwrapped. The home gateway also needs basic IPv6 security features.
